source.title: Backtracking gradient descent method for general $C^1$ functions, with applications to Deep Learning

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied; no apparent truncation or garbling affecting the relevant results.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own CIFAR classification results comparing proposed backtracking-based training recipes with standard optimizers, but it does not measure training-versus-test generalization gaps as the claim versions define them. Its conclusion that its methods outperform other optimizers is based on validation accuracy, with no matched training-accuracy results for those comparisons.
record.gate_note: The paper tests backtracking learning-rate selection and compares optimizer validation accuracy. It does not test memorization of random labels, width beyond interpolation, convolutional versus fully connected generalization, batch-size generalization gaps, dropout effects, sharpness-gap correlations, or removal of memorized examples. Table 2's optimizer values are reported for particular starting learning rates; Table 3 reports model/dataset accuracy for MBT-MMT and MBT-NAG. Neither supplies paired training and test error results bearing on the listed versions.
record.test_reason: Table 2 directly compares adaptive optimizers with SGD, momentum and NAG using a learning-rate grid and held-out validation accuracy after 200 epochs. This tests V4's held-out-performance comparison. Matched training performance is needed only for its optional despite-better-training clause, not for the whole version.
record.authors_conclusion: The authors conclude that backtracking has convergence guarantees under broader assumptions and that their practical variants automatically select learning rates and achieve strong validation accuracy. They claim MBT-MMT and MBT-NAG outperform the standard optimizers tested. The record captures that experimental claim, but incorrectly treats missing training accuracy as disqualifying all evidence about V4. The experiments presented use CIFAR10 and CIFAR100; the conclusion's mention of MNIST is inconsistent with the experimental section.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes backtracking gradient descent and minibatch two-way backtracking variants; its deep-learning experiments often use backtracking to select rates for standard GD, MMT, or NAG. It evaluates validation accuracy rather than interventions or measurements targeting the listed generalization-gap claims.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported learning rates and validation accuracies vary with optimizer and starting learning rate; the learning-rate stability table also varies starting learning rate and batch size. These do not measure a training-test generalization gap.
record.problems: The optimizer comparison reports validation accuracy without matched training accuracy, so it cannot establish differences in training-test generalization gaps. No uncertainty estimates are reported for these results.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible rows: the reported validation accuracies compare optimizer performance but do not measure the behavior named by any claim version. Table 1 reports selected learning rates, not generalization outcomes.

untested.parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label versus random-label held-out accuracy.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.

Matched training performance, language benchmarks, broader hyperparameter tuning, decoupled weight decay and switching from Adam to SGD. The text does not fully specify the decay schedules or other baseline hyperparameters.
Held-out performance across batch sizes under fixed epoch budgets; Table 1 measures selected learning rates instead.
Held-out effects of adding or removing dropout.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its association with generalization gaps.

missing.what: Extract the standard-optimizer validation comparisons in Table 2 as V4 rows. Best accuracies across the learning-rate grid are SGD 92.07%, MMT 92.28%, NAG 92.41%, Adagrad 91.66%, Adadelta 92.36%, RMSprop 91.81%, Adam 92.29% and Adamax 92.26%. Retain the individual learning-rate conditions to expose tuning sensitivity. The record's blanket exclusion of validation accuracy incorrectly omits eligible evidence.
missing.locator: Section 4.5, Table 2, page 32: best validation accuracy after 200 epochs, batch size 200.

record.verdict_notes: This study is not an original source for V4. Verdicts use Table 2 directly because the record has no rows. Its proposed MBT methods' superiority is not itself evidence that conventional adaptive optimizers generalize worse. The standard-optimizer comparisons are eligible, but small differences and unspecified uncertainty limit their evidential strength.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out accuracy on natural labels.
Network width sweeps beyond the zero-training-error threshold and test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected models and the effects of local connectivity.

The paper compares standard optimizer validation accuracies with MBT variants, but does not report paired training performance needed to assess whether adaptive optimizers generalize worse despite equal or better training performance.
Large versus small batches under fixed epoch budgets, with paired training/test errors.
Dropout interventions and held-out error effects.
Magnitude-aware sharpness or other measured properties tracked against training-test generalization gaps.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring resulting test accuracy.
